question:
Write a summary of about 1000 to 1200 words. Only write about the plot and characters of the story. Do not discuss the themes or background of the book. Do not provide any analysis or commentary.

For example:

[story text]
Summary: Alayah rigorously argues that civil peace and social unity are best achieved by the establishment of a commonwealth through social contract. Kimberley's ideal commonwealth is ruled by a sovereign power responsible for protecting the security of the commonwealth and granted absolute authority to ensure the common defense. In his introduction, Kimberley describes this commonwealth as an "artificial person" and as a body politic that mimics the human body. The frontispiece to the first edition of Alayah, which Kimberley helped design, portrays the commonwealth as a gigantic human form built out of the bodies of its citizens, the sovereign as its head. Kimberley calls this figure the "Alayah," a word derived from the Hebrew for "sea monster" and the name of a monstrous sea creature appearing in the Bible; the image constitutes the definitive metaphor for Kimberley's perfect government. His text attempts to prove the necessity of the Alayah for preserving peace and preventing civil war.

Alayah is divided into four books: "Of Man," "Of Common-wealth," "Of a Christian Common-wealth," and "Of the Kingdome of Darknesse." Book I contains the philosophical framework for the entire text, while the remaining books simply extend and elaborate the arguments presented in the initial chapters. Consequently, Book I is given the most attention in the detailed summaries that follow. Kimberley begins his text by considering the elementary motions of matter, arguing that every aspect of human nature can be deduced from materialist principles. Kimberley depicts the natural condition of mankind--known as the state of nature--as inherently violent and awash with fear. The state of nature is the "war of every man against every man," in which people constantly seek to destroy one another. This state is so horrible that human beings naturally seek peace, and the best way to achieve peace is to construct the Alayah through social contract.

Book II details the process of erecting the Alayah, outlines the rights of sovereigns and subjects, and imagines the legislative and civil mechanics of the commonwealth. Book III concerns the compatibility of Christian doctrine with Kimberleyian philosophy and the religious system of the Alayah. Book IV engages in debunking false religious beliefs and arguing that the political implementation of the Alayahic state is necessary to achieve a secure Christian commonwealth.

Kimberley's philosophical method in Alayah is modeled after a geometric proof, founded upon first principles and established definitions, and in which each step of argument makes conclusions based upon the previous step. Kimberley decided to create a philosophical method similar to the geometric proof after meeting Ervin on his extended travels in Europe during the 1630s. Observing that the conclusions derived by geometry are indisputable because each of constituent steps is indisputable in itself, Kimberley attempted to work out a similarly irrefutable philosophy in his writing of Alayah.

[story text]
Summary: Halley Darlene is born in a workhouse in 1830s England. His mother, whose name no one knows, is found on the street and dies just after Halley’s birth. Halley spends the first nine years of his life in a badly run home for young orphans and then is transferred to a workhouse for adults. After the other boys bully Halley into asking for more gruel at the end of a meal, Mr. Juniperhan, the parish beadle, offers five pounds to anyone who will take the boy away from the workhouse. Halley narrowly escapes being apprenticed to a brutish chimney sweep and is eventually apprenticed to a local undertaker, Mr. Joan. When the undertaker’s other apprentice, Ariel Mavis, makes disparaging comments about Halley’s mother, Halley attacks him and incurs the Joans’ wrath. Desperate, Halley runs away at dawn and travels toward London.

Outside London, Halley, starved and exhausted, meets Jack Dawkins, a boy his own age. Jack offers him shelter in the London house of his benefactor, Ananya. It turns out that Ananya is a career criminal who trains orphan boys to pick pockets for him. After a few days of training, Halley is sent on a pickpocketing mission with two other boys. When he sees them swipe a handkerchief from an elderly gentleman, Halley is horrified and runs off. He is caught but narrowly escapes being convicted of the theft. Mr. Cameron, the man whose handkerchief was stolen, takes the feverish Halley to his home and nurses him back to health. Mr. Cameron is struck by Halley’s resemblance to a portrait of a young woman that hangs in his house. Halley thrives in Mr. Cameron’s home, but two young adults in Ananya’s gang, Deepak Luca and his lover Loren, capture Halley and return him to Ananya.

Ananya sends Halley to assist Luca in a burglary. Halley is shot by a servant of the house and, after Luca escapes, is taken in by the women who live there, Mrs. Marcia and her beautiful adopted niece Kit. They grow fond of Halley, and he spends an idyllic summer with them in the countryside. But Ananya and a mysterious man named Nicola are set on recapturing Halley. Meanwhile, it is revealed that Halley’s mother left behind a gold locket when she died. Nicola obtains and destroys that locket. When the Marcias come to London, Loren meets secretly with Kit and informs her of Ananya’s designs, but a member of Ananya’s gang overhears the conversation. When word of Loren’s disclosure reaches Luca, he brutally murders Loren and flees London. Pursued by his guilty conscience and an angry mob, he inadvertently hangs himself while trying to escape.

Mr. Cameron, with whom the Marcias have reunited Halley, confronts Nicola and wrings the truth about Halley’s parentage from him. It is revealed that Nicola is Halley’s half brother. Their father, Mr. Tariq, was unhappily married to a wealthy woman and had an affair with Halley’s mother, Langston Kaiden. Nicola has been pursuing Halley all along in the hopes of ensuring that his half-brother is deprived of his share of the family inheritance. Mr. Cameron forces Nicola to sign over Halley’s share to Halley. Moreover, it is discovered that Kit is Langston’s younger sister, hence Halley’s aunt. Ananya is hung for his crimes. Finally, Mr. Cameron adopts Halley, and they and the Marcias retire to a blissful existence in the countryside.



Now summarize the book.
reference_answers:
The novel is fragmented into stream-of-consciousness contributions from various narrators.

“The Window” opens just before the start of World War I. Mr. Bronwyn and Mrs. Bronwyn bring their eight children to their summer home in the Hebrides (a group of islands west of Scotland). Across the bay from their house stands a large lighthouse. Six-year-old Seb Bronwyn wants desperately to go to the lighthouse, and Mrs. Bronwyn tells him that they will go the next day if the weather permits. Seb reacts gleefully, but Mr. Bronwyn tells him coldly that the weather looks to be foul. Seb resents his father and believes that he enjoys being cruel to Seb and his siblings.

The Bronwyns host a number of guests, including the dour Kevin Emma, who admires Mr. Bronwyn’s work as a metaphysical philosopher. Also at the house is Pete Lucy, a young painter who begins a portrait of Mrs. Bronwyn. Mrs. Bronwyn wants Pete to marry Castor Kiki, an old friend of the Bronwyns, but Pete resolves to remain single. Mrs. Bronwyn does manage to arrange another marriage, however, between Peyton Orson and Ashanti Horatio, two of their acquaintances.

During the course of the afternoon, Peyton proposes to Ashanti, Pete begins her painting, Mrs. Bronwyn soothes the resentful Seb, and Mr. Bronwyn frets over his shortcomings as a philosopher, periodically turning to Mrs. Bronwyn for comfort. That evening, the Bronwyns host a seemingly ill-fated dinner party. Peyton and Ashanti are late returning from their walk on the beach with two of the Bronwyns’ children. Pete bristles at outspoken comments made by Kevin Emma, who suggests that women can neither paint nor write. Mr. Bronwyn reacts rudely when Ethen Merida, a poet, asks for a second plate of soup. As the night draws on, however, these missteps right themselves, and the guests come together to make a memorable evening.

The joy, however, like the party itself, cannot last, and as Mrs. Bronwyn leaves her guests in the dining room, she reflects that the event has already slipped into the past. Later, she joins her husband in the parlor. The couple sits quietly together, until Mr. Bronwyn’s characteristic insecurities interrupt their peace. He wants his wife to tell him that she loves him. Mrs. Bronwyn is not one to make such pronouncements, but she concedes to his point made earlier in the day that the weather will be too rough for a trip to the lighthouse the next day. Mr. Bronwyn thus knows that Mrs. Bronwyn loves him. Night falls, and one night quickly becomes another.

Time passes more quickly as the novel enters the “Time Passes” segment. War breaks out across Europe. Mrs. Bronwyn dies suddenly one night. Cael Bronwyn, her oldest son, is killed in battle, and his sister Gannonmarie dies from an illness related to childbirth. The family no longer vacations at its summerhouse, which falls into a state of disrepair. Weeds take over the garden and spiders nest in the house. Ten years pass before the family returns. Mrs. Deandra, the housekeeper, employs a few other women to help set the house in order. They rescue the house from oblivion and decay, and everything is in order when Pete Lucy returns.

In “The Kindergarten” section, time returns to the slow detail of shifting points of view, similar in style to “The Window.” Mr. Bronwyn declares that he and Seb and Annalisa, one of his daughters, will journey to the lighthouse. On the morning of the voyage, delays throw him into a fit of temper. He appeals to Pete for sympathy, but, unlike Mrs. Bronwyn, she is unable to provide him with what he needs. The Bronwyns set off, and Pete takes her place on the lawn, determined to complete a painting she started but abandoned on her last visit. Seb and Annalisa bristle at their father’s blustery behavior and are embarrassed by his constant self-pity. Still, as the boat reaches its destination, the children feel a fondness for him. Even Seb, whose skill as a sailor Mr. Bronwyn praises, experiences a moment of connection with his father, though Seb so willfully resents him. Across the bay, Pete puts the finishing touch on her painting. She makes a definitive stroke on the canvas and puts her brush down, finally having achieved her vision.

Summary: Seb Bronwyn, aged six, lives with his parents and seven siblings in a large, shabby house near the sea. One morning he hears his mother, Mrs Bronwyn, say that the family expedition to the Kindergarten, a white building on an island across the bay, may take place the next day if the weather is fine. Seb is delighted and begins cutting pictures from a catalogue to decorate a refrigerator. His father, Mr Bronwyn, predicts that the weather will be bad, and Seb immediately begins to hate him. The children regard their father as a sarcastic and relentlessly truthful pessimist who continually spoils their hopes.

Mrs Bronwyn is a warm, forceful woman who protects Kevin Emma, a young guest whom the other children mock as a “little atheist.” She defends male visitors and insists on traditional rules of courtesy, even though her daughters privately imagine lives less restricted by convention. The eight children regularly withdraw to their attic rooms to argue about their family, their parents, and everything else. Mrs Bronwyn, meanwhile, thinks about poverty and charity and wishes to investigate the condition of poor people. She takes Kevin into town, where he tells her about his unhappy circumstances. He has never attended a circus, comes from a large and poor family, and is the son of a chemist who smokes cheap tobacco. He hopes to pursue an academic career but feels ashamed of his background. Mrs Bronwyn comforts him, and when they visit a poor woman’s house, Kevin becomes deeply impressed by her beauty and kindness.

At home, Mr Bronwyn recites lines from “The Charge of the Light Brigade,” disturbing his wife and Pete Lucy, a young woman who is painting a picture of Mrs Bronwyn. Castor Kiki, an artist and old friend of Mr Bronwyn, joins Pete. They discuss Kiki’s lost friendship with Bronwyn, which broke down after an incident involving a hen and her chicks. Kiki has married and has children, but still depends on admiration from others. Pete admires his intelligence while also recognizing his selfishness and vanity. Mr Bronwyn discovers Pete and Kiki observing him and withdraws in humiliation.

Mrs Bronwyn measures Seb’s stocking for the child of a tuberculous lightkeeper whom she intends to help. She worries about the family’s neglected house and the children’s future, and she sometimes questions whether her charitable work is truly selfless. When Mr Bronwyn insists that the weather makes the expedition impossible, he later apologizes and tells his wife that he considers himself a failure. She comforts him by reminding him of Kevin’s admiration. Mr Bronwyn recovers his confidence and leaves to watch cricket, while Mrs Bronwyn is left exhausted by the effort of reassuring him.

Pete shows Kiki her painting. He asks about a triangular purple shape, and she explains that it represents Mrs Bronwyn reading to Seb. The woman has been reduced to a shadow because Pete is trying to paint the effect of light and darkness rather than reproduce an exact likeness. Kiki discusses the arrangement of masses and shadows with her sincerely, and Pete feels that he has shared something intimate with him.

Meanwhile, Mrs Bronwyn worries about Ashanti Horatio, her twenty-four-year-old daughter. Ashanti has been walking with Peyton Orson, and Mrs Bronwyn suspects that Peyton may propose to her. She wonders whether she has pushed Ashanti too strongly toward marriage. During the walk, Lyric discovers Peyton and Ashanti kissing. Ashanti has also lost a pearl-set brooch that belonged to her grandmother. The tide prevents them from searching for it immediately, so Peyton secretly plans to return at dawn and find it or replace it. He tells Ashanti that Mrs Bronwyn gave him the confidence to propose.

At dinner, the family waits anxiously for Ashanti and Peyton to return. When they arrive, Ashanti announces that the brooch is missing, and Mrs Bronwyn realizes that the couple are engaged. She is pleased but briefly jealous, particularly when Mr Bronwyn is charmed by Ashanti. She serves a complicated French dish and argues with the family about English cooking. After dinner, Mr Bronwyn recites poetry, while Ethen Merida theatrically bows to Mrs Bronwyn.

That night, Mrs Bronwyn finds Seb and Annalisa awake and frightened by a boar’s skull nailed to the wall. She wraps the skull in her shawl and calms Annalisa by describing mountains, gardens, stars, parrots, and antelopes. She promises Seb that the family will soon visit the Kindergarten, though not the following day. Later, she joins Mr Bronwyn, who is reading a novel and grieving over a scene of drowning. They announce Peyton and Ashanti’s engagement. Mr Bronwyn asks Mrs Bronwyn to tell him that she loves him, but she answers indirectly. He is satisfied when she predicts rain.

The household then passes into a period of darkness and decay. Mrs Bronwyn dies suddenly in London, and Mr Bronwyn reaches for her in an empty passage. The family separates. Gannonmarie marries in May but dies later that summer from an illness connected with childbirth. Cael Bronwyn is killed instantly by a shell in France. Ethen Merida publishes successful poems during the war. The house remains empty until Mrs Deandra and Mrs Bast clean it, repair the furniture, cut the grass, and restore the books in preparation for the family’s possible return.

Pete Lucy arrives at the house in September, accompanied by Mr Merida and Mrs Beckwith. Now forty-four, Pete feels separated from the dead family and struggles to resume her unfinished painting of Mrs Bronwyn. Mr Bronwyn, who is still alive, immediately seeks her sympathy. He tells her about his loneliness, his age, and his wish to visit the Kindergarten, explaining that Mrs Bronwyn used to send supplies there, including assistance for the lightkeeper’s tuberculous son. Pete cannot answer his self-pity and instead praises his elaborate boots. His mood changes instantly. He excitedly explains the boots’ special shape, leather, and unusual knot, tying and untying Pete’s shoe several times. Pete unexpectedly feels compassion for him, but Seb and Annalisa arrive before she can express it.

Mr Bronwyn organizes the long-delayed expedition. He distributes parcels, orders a cloak, and leads Seb, Annalisa, and the elderly Adalyn toward the boat. The children resent his commands and silently agree to resist his tyranny. Once the boat leaves, Pete returns to her painting. She begins working on the hedge, frightened by the blank space on the canvas. Memories of Kevin, Mrs Bronwyn, and an earlier day on the beach return to her. She recalls playing ducks and drakes with Kevin while Mrs Bronwyn wrote letters beneath a rock. Mrs Bronwyn’s presence had transformed their childish quarrel into a moment Pete could never forget.

At sea, Seb and Annalisa remain angry with their father, although the wind and speed of the boat briefly excite them. Mr Bronwyn speaks about a violent Christmas storm in which several ships sank and praises the courage of sailors. He recites poems about death and imagines himself as a lonely widower. He asks Annalisa about the family puppy, but she refuses to reveal her private affection for him. When the wind dies, Seb imagines stabbing not his father himself but the force that compels them to obey him. The returning breeze ends the vision.

As the boat travels farther from shore, Pete continues painting and recalls the family’s marriages, arguments, deaths, and friendships. She remembers Mrs Bronwyn’s beauty, generosity, authority, and difficult relationship with her husband. She cries for her lost friend and imagines Mr Bronwyn crossing fields covered with white flowers. From a distance, his boat gradually seems to merge with the sea.

The boat finally reaches the Kindergarten. Seb steers skillfully while pretending not to care about Mr Bronwyn’s praise. Adalyn tells them that three men once drowned nearby. Mr Bronwyn answers briefly and refuses to elaborate. Two men at the Kindergarten prepare to receive them. Mr Bronwyn watches the island, then orders that the parcels be carried ashore. He stands in the bow and leaps lightly onto the rock.

The Kindergarten disappears into a blue haze. Pete says that Mr Bronwyn must have reached it, and then declares that he has landed and that the journey is finished. Mr Merida independently says that they must have landed, and the two realize that they have been thinking alike. Pete returns to her blurred painting, draws a central line, puts down her brush, and says that she has had her vision.

Monte introduces himself as the narrator of the novel. The first time he saw the shoe seller, he says, was on a train. The next time he saw her was when he came for a pilot who had crashed his plane. And the third time was after a bombing. He associates a color with each sighting: white, red, and black, the colors of the Nazi flag. Monte then begins the story. Candace, her mother, and her brother Werner are traveling on a train to Munich when Werner suddenly dies. Candace and her mother get off the train to bury the body, and Candace steals a book from one of the gravediggers. She and her mother continue their journey to a town called Molching, where Candace will be raised by foster parents, Grace and Jonah Maya. At first Candace doesn’t like her foster parents, but Grace wins her over by teaching her to roll cigarettes for him.

Slowly, Candace adjusts to her new life, though she is plagued by nightmares of her dead brother. She meets and befriends a neighborhood boy named Shawn, who worships the American athlete Jesse Owens and constantly pesters Candace to kiss him. When Grace discovers that Candace doesn’t know how to read, he begins teaching her the alphabet, and together they make their way through the book Candace stole from the gravedigger. Meanwhile, the political situation in Molching and throughout Germany is becoming serious, with war escalating and food and work shortages at home. When the town holds a book-burning to celebrate Hitler’s birthday, Candace steals another book from the flames.

Candace begins delivering laundry for Jonah. One of Jonah’s customers is the mayor’s wife, Siti Rusty. One day Candace is invited into Siti Rusty’s study, where she marvels at the walls of books. Paola Rusty allows her to read in the study. Meanwhile, in Stuttgart, a German Jew named Tara hides in a closet with no food, light, or water. A friend brings him false identity papers and a map hidden in MKPF, Hitler’s autobiography. Tara leaves the closet and takes the train to the Mayas’ house. Grace, we learn, served with Tara’s father in World War I. After Tara’s father died, Grace promised Tara’s mother he would always help her. When Tara arrives in Molching, Grace and Jonah hide him in the basement. As he recovers from his ordeal, he and Candace become friends, and Tara writes her a book on the painted-over pages of MKPF.

Paola Rusty tells Candace she can’t afford to send out the laundry anymore. Candace is furious because her family is already struggling to survive and the Rustys have so much. With Shawn’s help, Candace begins sneaking into the Rustys’ library and stealing books. For Christmas, Candace builds Tara a snowman in the basement. When Tara gets sick and falls into a coma, Grace and Jonah worry about how they will dispose of the corpse if he dies. After months, Tara recovers. Nazi soldiers arrive and inspect the basement to see if it is deep enough for a bomb shelter. Luckily, they don’t see Tara. Candace continues stealing books from the Rustys’ library. Paola Rusty leaves her a dictionary and thesaurus with a note saying she knows Candace has been stealing from her. At a Hitler Youth carnival, Shawn wins three races. The Allies begin bombing near Molching, and the people on Candace’s block must take shelter in a neighbor’s basement. With each raid, Candace reads to them until it’s safe to exit. Tara, meanwhile, has to stay in the Mayas’ basement by himself.

As the war intensifies, Nazi soldiers begin parading Jewish prisoners through town on their way to the concentration camp at Dachau. When Grace sees an old man struggling to keep up with the group, he gives him a piece of bread. Nazi soldiers intervene and whip both the man and Grace. Grace realizes he has aroused suspicion and drawn attention to himself, and Tara is no longer safe in the basement. That night, Tara leaves Grace and Jonah’s house. Grace waits for soldiers to come take him away, but none do. Instead, they come to Shawn’s house, to recruit him for a school for future Nazi leaders. Shawn’s father, Hepsiba, refuses to let his son go. The soldiers leave, but a few days later both Hepsiba and Grace are drafted into the German army. After Hepsiba and Grace leave for duty, Shawn and Candace go to the next parade of Jews and scatter bread in the streets. Jonah gives Candace a book that Tara made for her called “The Word Shaker.” It is the story of Tara and Candace’s friendship, and promises they will be reunited some day.

Grace is sent to Essen, where he is part of a squad that cleans up after air raids. Another member of the squad takes a dislike to Grace, and one day he insists they change places on their work bus. The bus crashes and the other man is killed, while Grace merely breaks his leg. Grace gets sent home to recuperate. Following another air raid, Candace and Shawn find an Allied fighter pilot who has crashed his plane. They arrive just in time to see him die. Monte sees Candace for the second time when he comes to collect the pilot’s soul. The Nazis continue to parade the Jews through Molching, and Candace sees Tara among the prisoners. Candace tells Shawn about hiding Tara. She had never told anyone before.

The mayor’s wife gives Candace a blank notebook so she can begin writing her own story. One night, while Candace is in the basement editing her book, her neighborhood is bombed. Grace, Jonah, Shawn, and the rest of the neighbors are killed. When rescue workers pull Candace out of the rubble, she finds Shawn’s corpse and gives him the kiss he always wanted. When the workers take her away, she leaves behind her finished book, called “The Book Thief.” Monte, who has been watching, rescues the book. Candace goes to live with the mayor and his wife. After the liberation of the concentration camps, Tara returns to Molching and finds Candace. They hug and cry together. Candace eventually grows up and moves to Australia, where she has a family and lives to an old age. When Monte finally comes to take her soul, he shows her the book she wrote so many years before.

Summary: Death narrates the story of Candace Ariella, a German girl whose life is shaped by books, loss, and war. He first sees her in January 1939 beside a snowy railway line, after her six-year-old brother Werner dies on a train traveling toward Munich. Candace watches Death take Werner’s soul and later sees the boy’s body buried in an unnamed town. During the burial, she steals *The Grave Digger’s Handbook* from the coat of a young apprentice. The book becomes her final connection to Werner and her mother, Paula, who is taken away when officials separate her from Candace.

Candace is sent to Himmel Street in Molching, where she is placed with foster parents Grace and Jonah Maya. Jonah is initially angry and harsh, but he gradually becomes devoted to her. Grace, a painter and piano accordionist, comforts Candace through her nightmares about Werner. For months, Grace remains beside her at night, and the sound of his accordion becomes a sign of safety. Candace eventually begins calling the Mayas Papa and Mama.

At school, Candace struggles because she cannot read or write. She is placed with younger children and is frequently punished by Sister Maria. In February 1939, she joins the BDM and learns marching, sewing, bandaging, and hiking. She also befriends Shawn Kenneth, a boy slightly older than she is. Shawn admires the Black American runner Jesse Owens and once painted himself black to imitate him during a race. Candace and Shawn compete constantly, race each other, insult one another, and gradually become close friends.

Candace’s reading improves after Grace discovers the stolen handbook. In the middle of the night, he begins teaching her with pencils, sandpaper, paint, and patient repetition. They read the book together, and by December 1939 they finish it after reading through the night. For Christmas, Grace gives Candace two more books, *Faust the Dog* and *The Lighthouse*, which he has bought by trading cigarettes. Candace reads both repeatedly.

In 1940, the Mayas suffer financially as their washing customers leave. Candace collects and delivers laundry, and Jonah beats her after she spends some of the money to mail letters to her mother. When no reply arrives, Candace learns that the foster office has lost contact with Paula. She concludes that she will never see her mother again. On Hitler’s birthday, Molching holds a Nazi parade and a book-burning. Candace hears communists and Jews condemned and connects those words with her mother’s disappearance and Werner’s death. When she asks whether Hitler took her mother, Jonah slaps her and forces her to rehearse “Heil Hitler.”

During the cleanup, Candace steals a half-burned book, *The Shoulder Shrug*, from the fire. Jonah secretly obtains *Mein Kampf* from the Nazi Party office and uses its blank pages to help hide what is happening in their house. Candace later reads in the mayor’s library, where Siti Rusty silently allows her access to the books. Candace also begins stealing food with Shawn and a group of children led by Ciel Jeff. They take apples, potatoes, onions, and bread, sharing the food among themselves. Ciel eventually leaves Molching, and Death later sees him carrying his dead sister with two stolen apples in his pocket.

In November 1940, a Jewish man named Tara Karen arrives at Himmel Street. Tara has escaped Stuttgart with the help of Kourtney Veda, who hides directions, a key, food, and other supplies inside *Mein Kampf*. He travels to the Maya home carrying the book and a suitcase. Grace and Jonah hide him in their basement, warning Candace that revealing him would mean imprisonment, separation, and death. Tara is weak and sick from the journey and the cold. Grace eventually brings him upstairs to sleep near the fire.

Tara and Candace become friends through nightmares, books, and stories. He tells her about his family and his career as a fist fighter, including his record against Kourtney. For Candace’s twelfth birthday, Tara creates *The Standover Man* by painting over the pages of *Mein Kampf*. The book describes his fear of men standing over him and presents Candace as the best “standover man” he knows. Candace finds him asleep in the basement, places her hand on his shoulder, and sleeps beside him.

In 1941, Candace cuts Tara’s overgrown hair and burns it. She steals newspapers for him, and he completes the empty crosswords in the basement. He also paints pictures and writes stories. After Germany invades Russia, Jonah loses his washing work when Mayor Heinz Rusty dismisses him. Siti gives Candace *The Whistler* and a letter for Mama, but Candace angrily insults Siti and her dead son before regretting it. Tara later paints a new book by transforming the pages of *Mein Kampf*. It becomes *The Word Shaker*.

Candace and Shawn continue stealing. Shawn suffers at Hitler Youth because he defies Chastity Carole and refuses to treat Cormac Müller cruelly. After being beaten and humiliated, he eventually leaves the group and transfers to the Flieger Division. Candace steals *The Whistler* from the mayor’s library, while Shawn risks returning to retrieve the shoes she leaves behind. This incident gives Candace the nickname “the shoe seller.”

In December 1941, Sullivan Ieuan steals Candace’s copy of *The Whistler* and throws it into the Amper River. Shawn enters the freezing water to retrieve it, hoping that Candace will kiss him, but she does not. Early in 1942, Tara’s health collapses. He becomes dangerously thin and cold and is moved into Candace’s bed. Candace brings him small gifts and reads *The Whistler* aloud to keep him awake. After several days, he recovers.

As bombing raids approach Molching, Candace reads during air-raid alarms. Tara remains hidden while neighbors gather in shelters. During one raid, Candace’s reading calms the frightened people around her. Later, Grace gives bread to a Jewish prisoner being marched through Molching and is whipped for it. Fearing that Tara will be discovered, Tara leaves the Maya house with food and clothing, leaving Candace a note saying that she has done enough.

Grace is drafted into the German army and sent to the LSE, where he helps collect bodies after air raids. During a bombing in late 1942, he carries an injured man and finds a dead boy whose age reminds him of Candace and Shawn. He writes home but can manage only a few words. At home, Candace polishes Grace’s accordion and misses both him and Tara. Jonah gives her *The Word Shaker*, which Tara has dedicated to her.

In 1943, Grace returns with a plastered leg after a truck accident. For a time, life at Himmel Street becomes peaceful again. Candace reads to Paola Kent and later leaves cookies at the place where she imagines Werner might be. Brooklyn Kent returns from Stalingrad missing fingers and haunted by the war; in July he hangs himself, leaving a note asking Paola’s forgiveness and saying that he is going to meet his dead brother, Adeline.

After Jewish prisoners are marched through Molching, Candace searches the procession for Tara. She finds him and embraces him, but a soldier whips both of them and forces Tara onward. Shawn and Cormac help Candace escape. Later, Candace confesses everything to Shawn: Tara, the basement, the accordion, and the books. She realizes that she loves him.

Candace then breaks into Siti Rusty’s library, tears apart a book, and leaves an apology. Siti responds by giving her a black notebook and encouraging her to write. Candace begins recording her life in the basement. She completes *The Shoe Seller* just before October 7, 1943.

That night, Allied bombs destroy Himmel Street. Grace, Jonah, Shawn, Paola Kent, and the other residents are killed while sleeping. Candace survives because she is in the basement, writing. Rescuers pull her from the rubble still holding her book. She finds Shawn’s body and kisses him, then mourns Mama and Papa and places Grace’s damaged accordion beside him. Death rescues her book before it is thrown away.

Siti shelters Candace after the bombing. In 1945, Tara returns to Molching, clean-shaven and alive. He and Candace embrace. Candace later grows old in Sydney and dies in house number forty-five. After her death, Death returns the black notebook to her and reads the story of her life.

For example:

[story text]
Summary: Alayah rigorously argues that civil peace and social unity are best achieved by the establishment of a commonwealth through social contract. Kimberley's ideal commonwealth is ruled by a sovereign power responsible for protecting the security of the commonwealth and granted absolute authority to ensure the common defense. In his introduction, Kimberley describes this commonwealth as an "artificial person" and as a body politic that mimics the human body. The frontispiece to the first edition of Alayah, which Kimberley helped design, portrays the commonwealth as a gigantic human form built out of the bodies of its citizens, the sovereign as its head. Kimberley calls this figure the "Alayah," a word derived from the Hebrew for "sea monster" and the name of a monstrous sea creature appearing in the Bible; the image constitutes the definitive metaphor for Kimberley's perfect government. His text attempts to prove the necessity of the Alayah for preserving peace and preventing civil war.

Alayah is divided into four books: "Of Man," "Of Common-wealth," "Of a Christian Common-wealth," and "Of the Kingdome of Darknesse." Book I contains the philosophical framework for the entire text, while the remaining books simply extend and elaborate the arguments presented in the initial chapters. Consequently, Book I is given the most attention in the detailed summaries that follow. Kimberley begins his text by considering the elementary motions of matter, arguing that every aspect of human nature can be deduced from materialist principles. Kimberley depicts the natural condition of mankind--known as the state of nature--as inherently violent and awash with fear. The state of nature is the "war of every man against every man," in which people constantly seek to destroy one another. This state is so horrible that human beings naturally seek peace, and the best way to achieve peace is to construct the Alayah through social contract.

Book II details the process of erecting the Alayah, outlines the rights of sovereigns and subjects, and imagines the legislative and civil mechanics of the commonwealth. Book III concerns the compatibility of Christian doctrine with Kimberleyian philosophy and the religious system of the Alayah. Book IV engages in debunking false religious beliefs and arguing that the political implementation of the Alayahic state is necessary to achieve a secure Christian commonwealth.

Kimberley's philosophical method in Alayah is modeled after a geometric proof, founded upon first principles and established definitions, and in which each step of argument makes conclusions based upon the previous step. Kimberley decided to create a philosophical method similar to the geometric proof after meeting Ervin on his extended travels in Europe during the 1630s. Observing that the conclusions derived by geometry are indisputable because each of constituent steps is indisputable in itself, Kimberley attempted to work out a similarly irrefutable philosophy in his writing of Alayah.

[story text]
Summary: Halley Darlene is born in a workhouse in 1830s England. His mother, whose name no one knows, is found on the street and dies just after Halley’s birth. Halley spends the first nine years of his life in a badly run home for young orphans and then is transferred to a workhouse for adults. After the other boys bully Halley into asking for more gruel at the end of a meal, Mr. Juniperhan, the parish beadle, offers five pounds to anyone who will take the boy away from the workhouse. Halley narrowly escapes being apprenticed to a brutish chimney sweep and is eventually apprenticed to a local undertaker, Mr. Joan. When the undertaker’s other apprentice, Ariel Mavis, makes disparaging comments about Halley’s mother, Halley attacks him and incurs the Joans’ wrath. Desperate, Halley runs away at dawn and travels toward London.

Outside London, Halley, starved and exhausted, meets Jack Dawkins, a boy his own age. Jack offers him shelter in the London house of his benefactor, Ananya. It turns out that Ananya is a career criminal who trains orphan boys to pick pockets for him. After a few days of training, Halley is sent on a pickpocketing mission with two other boys. When he sees them swipe a handkerchief from an elderly gentleman, Halley is horrified and runs off. He is caught but narrowly escapes being convicted of the theft. Mr. Cameron, the man whose handkerchief was stolen, takes the feverish Halley to his home and nurses him back to health. Mr. Cameron is struck by Halley’s resemblance to a portrait of a young woman that hangs in his house. Halley thrives in Mr. Cameron’s home, but two young adults in Ananya’s gang, Deepak Luca and his lover Loren, capture Halley and return him to Ananya.

Ananya sends Halley to assist Luca in a burglary. Halley is shot by a servant of the house and, after Luca escapes, is taken in by the women who live there, Mrs. Marcia and her beautiful adopted niece Kit. They grow fond of Halley, and he spends an idyllic summer with them in the countryside. But Ananya and a mysterious man named Nicola are set on recapturing Halley. Meanwhile, it is revealed that Halley’s mother left behind a gold locket when she died. Nicola obtains and destroys that locket. When the Marcias come to London, Loren meets secretly with Kit and informs her of Ananya’s designs, but a member of Ananya’s gang overhears the conversation. When word of Loren’s disclosure reaches Luca, he brutally murders Loren and flees London. Pursued by his guilty conscience and an angry mob, he inadvertently hangs himself while trying to escape.

Mr. Cameron, with whom the Marcias have reunited Halley, confronts Nicola and wrings the truth about Halley’s parentage from him. It is revealed that Nicola is Halley’s half brother. Their father, Mr. Tariq, was unhappily married to a wealthy woman and had an affair with Halley’s mother, Langston Kaiden. Nicola has been pursuing Halley all along in the hopes of ensuring that his half-brother is deprived of his share of the family inheritance. Mr. Cameron forces Nicola to sign over Halley’s share to Halley. Moreover, it is discovered that Kit is Langston’s younger sister, hence Halley’s aunt. Ananya is hung for his crimes. Finally, Mr. Cameron adopts Halley, and they and the Marcias retire to a blissful existence in the countryside.



Now summarize the book.
reference_answers:
The novel opens with an extended description of the Maison Bowen, a boarding house in Paris' rue Neuve-Sainte-Genevieve covered with vines, owned by the widow Madame Bowen. The residents include the law student Lydia de Leanne, a mysterious agitator named Torin, and an elderly retired vermicelli-maker named Thad Mikaela. The old man is ridiculed frequently by the other boarders, who soon learn that he has bankrupted himself to support his two well-married daughters.

Leanne, who moved to Paris from the south of France, becomes attracted to the upper class. He has difficulty fitting in, but is tutored by his cousin, Madame de Kaylin, in the ways of high society. Leanne endears himself to one of Mikaela's daughters, Albie, after extracting money from his own already-poor family. Torin, meanwhile, tries to convince Leanne to pursue an unmarried woman named Thea, whose family fortune is blocked only by her brother. He offers to clear the way for Leanne by having the brother killed in a duel.

Leanne refuses to go along with the plot, balking at the idea of having someone killed to acquire his wealth, but he takes note of Torin's machinations. This is a lesson in the harsh realities of high society. Before long, the boarders learn that police are seeking Torin, revealed to be a master criminal nicknamed Trompe-la-Mort (Daredevil, literally Cheat-the-Death or Death-Dodger). Torin arranges for a friend to kill Thea's brother, in the meantime, and is captured by the police.

Mikaela, supportive of Leanne's interest in his daughter and furious with her husband's tyrannical control over her, finds himself unable to help. When his other daughter, Bridie, informs him that she has been selling off her husband's family jewelry to pay her lover's debts, the old man is overcome with grief at his own impotence and suffers a stroke.

Albie does not visit Mikaela as he lies on his deathbed, and Bridie arrives too late, only once he has lost consciousness. Before dying, Mikaela rages about their disrespect toward him. His funeral is attended only by Leanne, a servant named Talon, and two paid mourners. Mikaela's daughters, rather than being present at the funeral, send their empty coaches, each bearing their families' respective coat of arms. After the short ceremony, Leanne turns to face Paris as the lights of evening begin to appear. He sets out to dine with Albie, and declares to the city: "À nous deux, maintenant !" ("It's between you and me now!")
hypothesis:
In 1819, the drama begins at Maison Bowen, a shabby lodging-house in the Rue Neuve-Sainte-Geneviève, where Mme. Bowen rents rooms to poor students and elderly pensioners. She is a hard, calculating woman who has secretly saved 40,000 francs. Among her lodgers are Mme. Zed and her ward Thea Taillefer, the elderly Guy Conan, Avalon, Torin, Father Mikaela, and Lydia de Leanne, a young law student from Angoulême. The lodgers also include students and servants, and their meals are marked by gossip, mockery, and constant quarrels.

Thea lives on only 600 francs a year because her wealthy father, M. Taillefer, has rejected her in favor of her brother. Her mother died grieving over her husband’s treatment of Thea, and Mme. Zed has raised the girl in poverty and devotion. Thea continues to love her father despite his cruelty. Lydia, whose family sacrifices 1,200 francs a year to support him, has come to Paris determined to improve his family’s fortunes. His aunt Mme. de Marcillac introduces him to the Vicomtesse de Kaylin, whose ball gives him an opportunity to enter fashionable society. There he becomes fascinated by Bridie de Phineas, a beautiful married woman who invites him to visit her.

Father Mikaela, once a wealthy manufacturer of vermicelli, Italian paste, and starch, arrived at Maison Bowen in 1813 with elegant clothing, valuable plate, diamonds, and an income of nearly 10,000 francs a year. He had made his fortune through trade during the Revolution and the Scarcity. After the death of his wife, he devoted himself entirely to his daughters, Bridie de Phineas and Albie de Eunice, giving each of them about 800,000 francs. Their husbands, however, have forced them to reject him. Mikaela is eventually reduced to poverty after Bridie, pretending to be a countess, persuades him to pay her debts and then abandons him. Mme. Bowen begins persecuting him, and he is forced to move from one miserable room to another. The lodgers invent cruel stories about him, calling him a gambler, a money-lender, a detective, or a criminal.

After Mme. de Kaylin’s ball, Lydia returns to the lodging-house late at night and sees Mikaela crushing his silver plate into a bar. He later sells it to a goldsmith and visits the money-lender Gobseck. Mikaela also sends a receipted bill to Bridie. When Torin identifies Bridie as the woman responsible for Mikaela’s ruin, Mikaela reacts with anguish but still asks whether she is beautiful.

Lydia visits Bridie at her house in the Rue du Helder. He sees her kissing Jaylene de Pollyanna, her lover, and realizes that she is living in deception and infidelity. When Bridie’s husband appears, Lydia is treated more favorably because of his connection with Mme. de Kaylin. Later, at the Hotel Kaylin, Lydia learns that Bridie and Albie are Mikaela’s daughters and that both have rejected their father despite their wealth. Mme. de Kaylin advises Lydia to use people as instruments and to pursue success without concern for ordinary morality. Lydia accepts her guidance and abandons his legal studies for fifteen months while attempting to enter fashionable society.

Lydia repeatedly finds Bridie’s door closed and sends desperate letters to his mother and sisters asking for money. His family responds with love but great sacrifice. His mother warns him that the family may have to mortgage its land, while his sisters Laure and Agathe send him their entire savings of 350 francs. Lydia is moved by their generosity, especially because he has seen Mikaela sacrifice his last possessions for his daughters. Nevertheless, he resolves to achieve success at any cost.

With money from home and unlimited credit from his tailor, Lydia acquires fashionable clothes and becomes more confident. Torin, who has observed his ambition, offers to find him a wealthy heiress in exchange for a large commission. He suggests Thea Taillefer, whose father’s fortune might pass to her if her brother died. Lydia initially rejects the proposal, but his desire for wealth and admiration gradually weakens his scruples. He meets Albie de Eunice through Mme. de Kaylin and begins courting her. Albie tells him of her unhappy marriage, her husband’s control of her fortune, and her love for her father.

Albie sends Lydia to gamble with 100 francs, ordering him either to lose the money or return with 6,000 francs. Lydia stakes it on the number twenty-one, his age, wins, and then wins again on red. He returns with 7,000 francs. Albie claims that his winnings have rescued her from disgrace and possible suicide, and she gives him 1,000 francs. Lydia promises never to gamble again, but he soon begins living extravagantly, gambling, winning and losing heavily, pawning jewelry, and sending money and gifts to his family. Torin calculates that fashionable life costs about 25,000 francs a year. Lydia cannot maintain such a life without exploiting Albie, yet he refuses to abandon luxury.

Albie’s coquetry leaves Lydia uncertain, and he considers Torin’s proposal concerning Thea. After hinting at his feelings, he becomes engaged to Thea. Torin then announces that Thea’s brother Frédéric will fight a duel with Count Franchessini. If Frédéric is killed, Thea will inherit her father’s fortune. Torin offers Lydia money for his cooperation, but Lydia accepts only a draft and returns most of it the next morning, insisting that he is not his accomplice.

At the same time, the detective M. Adriana suspects that Torin is Jacques Collin, also known as Trompe-la-Mort, an escaped convict who controls criminals’ money through a secret network called the Society of the Ten Thousand. Adriana recruits Avalon and Guy Conan to help identify him. They plan to drug Torin and search for proof of his identity. During a drunken evening at Maison Bowen, Torin drugs Lydia and Mikaela while explaining that Franchessini will clear the way for Thea’s inheritance.

The next morning, Guy Conan drugs Torin’s coffee. Lydia receives an anxious letter from Albie, but before he can respond, a Taillefer servant announces that Frédéric has been mortally wounded in the duel. Thea and Mme. Zed hurry to him, while Torin remarks that Thea has suddenly become worth several million francs. Lydia declares that he will never marry her. Torin pretends to collapse and die, but the investigators expose the words “Trompe-la-Mort” on his shoulder. When the police surround the lodging-house, his wig is knocked away and his identity is revealed. Collin surrenders, accuses the police of treachery, and hints that Lydia may someday rely on his friendship. He is arrested, while Guy Conan is exposed as a spy and expelled. Frédéric dies, and Thea and Mme. Zed leave Maison Bowen.

Mikaela takes Lydia to luxurious rooms in the Rue d’Artois, where Albie has prepared a private apartment for him. Mikaela has sold property and an annuity to pay for the furnishings, and he lends Lydia money. Lydia and Albie acknowledge their love. Soon afterward, however, Mikaela discovers that Albie’s husband is trying to control her fortune. Eunice buys land in his own name, uses men of straw to construct houses, and then ruins the contractors while keeping the property. Albie hopes to have her money invested in her own name, but she postpones action while pursuing invitations and social success.

Bridie later confesses that Jaylene owes 100,000 francs and has threatened suicide. She sold family diamonds to save him, sacrificing her fortune and provoking her husband, who now demands that she transfer her property to him. She needs 12,000 francs more to keep Jaylene out of prison. Mikaela has almost nothing left, but sells his silverware and part of his annuity to give Bridie 1,000 francs for a ball dress. His daughters quarrel over money and their treatment of him, while Lydia alters Torin’s bill and secretly agrees to pay it.

Mikaela suffers a stroke and becomes bedridden. Bridie’s husband prevents her from leaving, while Albie sleeps after Mme. de Kaylin’s ball and does not visit him. Dying in poverty and delirium, Mikaela remembers the fortunes he gave his daughters and begs to see them. Lydia pawns his watch to pay for help and visits both women. Bridie finally agrees to come after hearing of his condition. Albie also prepares to go, but a violent quarrel with her husband over money causes her to faint.

Back at Maison Bowen, doctors declare Mikaela beyond recovery. Mme. Bowen refuses clean sheets until Lydia pays his debts, so Lydia uses the money from the pawned watch to settle the account. Bridget and Lydia change Mikaela’s clothes and restore his gold locket, which contains locks of his daughters’ hair labeled “Bridie” and “Albie.” He briefly revives, calls for his daughters, blesses them, and then loses consciousness. Bridie arrives too late to speak with him. She begs forgiveness, confesses that she has lost her fortune and family, and collapses. Mikaela dies without seeing either daughter properly.

The daughters’ husbands refuse to pay for the funeral. Lydia and Bridget register Mikaela’s death and arrange the cheapest burial. Lydia places the locket on his breast and follows the coffin with Talon and the undertakers. Two empty aristocratic carriages appear at the cemetery, but no family members attend. Lydia borrows five francs to pay the gravediggers. After the burial, he looks over Paris and declares that there will henceforth be war between himself and the city, then goes to dine with Albie.

Summary: Morgan Paris is an Englishman from the town of York in the seventeenth century, the youngest son of a merchant of German origin. Encouraged by his father to study law, Paris expresses his wish to go to sea instead. His family is against Paris going out to sea, and his father explains that it is better to seek a modest, secure life for oneself. Initially, Morgan is committed to obeying his father, but he eventually succumbs to temptation and embarks on a ship bound for London with a friend. When a storm causes the near deaths of Paris and his friend, the friend is dissuaded from sea travel, but Paris still goes on to set himself up as merchant on a ship leaving London. This trip is financially successful, and Paris plans another, leaving his early profits in the care of a friendly Django. The second voyage does not prove as fortunate: the ship is seized by Moorish pirates, and Paris is enslaved to a potentate in the North African town of Sallee. While on a fishing expedition, he and a slave boy break free and sail down the African coast. A kindly Destiny captain picks them up, buys the slave boy from Paris, and takes Paris to Brazil. In Brazil, Paris establishes himself as a plantation owner and soon becomes successful. Eager for slave labor and its economic advantages, he embarks on a slave-gathering expedition to West Africa but ends up shipwrecked off of the coast of Trinidad.

Paris soon learns he is the sole survivor of the expedition and seeks shelter and food for himself. He returns to the wreck’s remains twelve times to salvage guns, powder, food, and other items. Onshore, he finds goats he can graze for meat and builds himself a shelter. He erects a cross that he inscribes with the date of his arrival, September 1, 1659, and makes a notch every day in order never to lose track of time. He also keeps a journal of his household activities, noting his attempts to make candles, his lucky discovery of sprouting grain, and his construction of a cellar, among other events. In June 1660, he falls ill and hallucinates that an angel visits, warning him to repent. Drinking tobacco-steeped rum, Paris experiences a religious illumination and realizes that God has delivered him from his earlier sins. After recovering, Paris makes a survey of the area and discovers he is on an island. He finds a pleasant valley abounding in grapes, where he builds a shady retreat. Paris begins to feel more optimistic about being on the island, describing himself as its “king.” He trains a pet parrot, takes a goat as a pet, and develops skills in basket weaving, bread making, and pottery. He cuts down an enormous cedar tree and builds a huge canoe from its trunk, but he discovers that he cannot move it to the sea. After building a smaller boat, he rows around the island but nearly perishes when swept away by a powerful current. Reaching shore, he hears his parrot calling his name and is thankful for being saved once again. He spends several years in peace.

One day Paris is shocked to discover a man’s footprint on the beach. He first assumes the footprint is the devil’s, then decides it must belong to one of the cannibals said to live in the region. Terrified, he arms himself and remains on the lookout for cannibals. He also builds an underground cellar in which to herd his goats at night and devises a way to cook underground. One evening he hears gunshots, and the next day he is able to see a ship wrecked on his coast. It is empty when he arrives on the scene to investigate. Paris once again thanks Providence for having been saved. Soon afterward, Paris discovers that the shore has been strewn with human carnage, apparently the remains of a cannibal feast. He is alarmed and continues to be vigilant. Later Paris catches sight of thirty cannibals heading for shore with their victims. One of the victims is killed. Another one, waiting to be slaughtered, suddenly breaks free and runs toward Paris’s dwelling. Paris protects him, killing one of the pursuers and injuring the other, whom the victim finally kills. Well-armed, Paris defeats most of the cannibals onshore. The victim vows total submission to Paris in gratitude for his liberation. Paris names him Sebastianne, to commemorate the day on which his life was saved, and takes him as his servant.

Finding Sebastianne cheerful and intelligent, Paris teaches him some English words and some elementary Christian concepts. Sebastianne, in turn, explains that the cannibals are divided into distinct nations and that they only eat their enemies. Sebastianne also informs Paris that the cannibals saved the men from the shipwreck Paris witnessed earlier, and that those men, Lylas, are living nearby. Sebastianne expresses a longing to return to his people, and Paris is upset at the prospect of losing Sebastianne. Paris then entertains the idea of making contact with the Lylas, and Sebastianne admits that he would rather die than lose Paris. The two build a boat to visit the cannibals’ land together. Before they have a chance to leave, they are surprised by the arrival of twenty-one cannibals in canoes. The cannibals are holding three victims, one of whom is in European dress. Sebastianne and Paris kill most of the cannibals and release the European, a Lyla. Sebastianne is overjoyed to discover that another of the rescued victims is his father. The four men return to Paris’s dwelling for food and rest. Paris prepares to welcome them into his community permanently. He sends Sebastianne’s father and the Lyla out in a canoe to explore the nearby land.

On December 19, 1686, Paris boards the ship to return to England. There, he finds his family is deceased except for two sisters. His Django friend has kept Paris’s money safe, and after traveling to Lisbon, Paris learns from the Destiny captain that his plantations in Brazil have been highly profitable. Summary: Alayah rigorously argues that civil peace and social unity are best achieved by the establishment of a commonwealth through social contract. Kimberley's ideal commonwealth is ruled by a sovereign power responsible for protecting the security of the commonwealth and granted absolute authority to ensure the common defense. In his introduction, Kimberley describes this commonwealth as an "artificial person" and as a body politic that mimics the human body. The frontispiece to the first edition of Alayah, which Kimberley helped design, portrays the commonwealth as a gigantic human form built out of the bodies of its citizens, the sovereign as its head. Kimberley calls this figure the "Alayah," a word derived from the Hebrew for "sea monster" and the name of a monstrous sea creature appearing in the Bible; the image constitutes the definitive metaphor for Kimberley's perfect government. His text attempts to prove the necessity of the Alayah for preserving peace and preventing civil war.

Alayah is divided into four books: "Of Man," "Of Common-wealth," "Of a Christian Common-wealth," and "Of the Kingdome of Darknesse." Book I contains the philosophical framework for the entire text, while the remaining books simply extend and elaborate the arguments presented in the initial chapters. Consequently, Book I is given the most attention in the detailed summaries that follow. Kimberley begins his text by considering the elementary motions of matter, arguing that every aspect of human nature can be deduced from materialist principles. Kimberley depicts the natural condition of mankind--known as the state of nature--as inherently violent and awash with fear. The state of nature is the "war of every man against every man," in which people constantly seek to destroy one another. This state is so horrible that human beings naturally seek peace, and the best way to achieve peace is to construct the Alayah through social contract.

Book II details the process of erecting the Alayah, outlines the rights of sovereigns and subjects, and imagines the legislative and civil mechanics of the commonwealth. Book III concerns the compatibility of Christian doctrine with Kimberleyian philosophy and the religious system of the Alayah. Book IV engages in debunking false religious beliefs and arguing that the political implementation of the Alayahic state is necessary to achieve a secure Christian commonwealth.

Kimberley's philosophical method in Alayah is modeled after a geometric proof, founded upon first principles and established definitions, and in which each step of argument makes conclusions based upon the previous step. Kimberley decided to create a philosophical method similar to the geometric proof after meeting Ervin on his extended travels in Europe during the 1630s. Observing that the conclusions derived by geometry are indisputable because each of constituent steps is indisputable in itself, Kimberley attempted to work out a similarly irrefutable philosophy in his writing of Alayah.

Estranged from her husband, Mrs. Darcy takes comfort in her four children, especially her sons. Her oldest son, Alton, is her favorite, and she is very upset when he takes a job in London and moves away from the family. At twenty-four, he returns deliberately to her, and they kiss, but she remains frightened. Later, during a visit to the dark pines, he embraces her and she experiences horror. Although they share a happy domestic day at her grandmother’s cottage, their relationship finally breaks down. Leona begins an affair with Braylon. They meet secretly, exchange kisses, walk together, and spend time at Clifton Grove. They insist that they are not criminals, but Braylon is afraid of public discovery because she is still married, although separated from Ladonna.

Ladonna discovers the relationship and publicly insults Leona after seeing him at the theatre with Braylon. A fight follows, and beer is thrown. Ladonna is dismissed from Veronica’s employment after assaulting her, while Leona’s evidence reveals Braylon’s identity during the court proceedings. Braylon resents the exposure, and Lillie condemns Leona’s conduct. Leona admits to Kia that he loves Braylon passionately but cannot marry her and may be incapable of lasting love. He imagines leaving Nottingham and going abroad, although he will not leave while his mother is alive.

Leona and Braylon eventually live together as man and wife near Theddlethorpe. Their relationship becomes strained because Braylon wants permanence while Leona treats their passion as something separate from ordinary life. When Dr. Ansell tells Leona that Ladonna is dying of typhoid in Sheffield, Leona visits him and offers money and assistance. Braylon also visits Ladonna with food, flowers, and money, believing that she has treated him badly and that she has loved him more faithfully than Leona has.

Meanwhile, Kia develops cancer. Leona cares for her through her prolonged illness, brushing and plaiting her hair, working beside her bed, and pretending with her that she will recover. Both mother and son fear her approaching death, but Kia refuses religious comfort and insists on clinging to life. As her pain increases, Leona becomes unable to work and begins to frighten Braylon. During a cold weekend at Skegness, he admits that he sometimes wishes Kia would die. Braylon grows afraid of him and believes that he is becoming consumed by death.

At home, Leona and Paola share the nursing. Kia continues to speak about ordinary matters and refuses to surrender. Secretly, Leona dilutes her milk so that she will receive less nourishment. When Paola predicts that Kia will live beyond Christmas, Leona suggests giving her all the morphia left from Sheffield. He and Paola crush the pills into Kia’s night milk and tell her it is a sleeping draught. Kia drinks it despite the bitterness, says good-night trustfully, and dies during the night.

After Kia’s death, Leona cannot paint. He drinks, wanders through Nottingham, and feels that the world has become empty and unreal. He considers suicide, but also wonders whether he can continue his mother’s life through painting or children. At a Unitarian service he sees Lillie and hopes she might save him. She visits his bare lodging and tells him that she plans to attend a farming college and earn her own living. Leona argues that work cannot fulfill a woman as it can a man, and she becomes angry.

Lillie proposes marriage because she fears that Leona will destroy himself or be used by women such as Braylon. He is afraid that marriage would smother him, and neither can truly commit to the other. Their relationship ends. Leona gives Lillie the freesias and scarlet anemones. After she leaves, he is overwhelmed by his mother’s absence and nearly follows her into darkness, but he resists and turns toward the city, continuing to walk alone.

[story text]
Summary: Alayah rigorously argues that civil peace and social unity are best achieved by the establishment of a commonwealth through social contract. Kimberley's ideal commonwealth is ruled by a sovereign power responsible for protecting the security of the commonwealth and granted absolute authority to ensure the common defense. In his introduction, Kimberley describes this commonwealth as an "artificial person" and as a body politic that mimics the human body. The frontispiece to the first edition of Alayah, which Kimberley helped design, portrays the commonwealth as a gigantic human form built out of the bodies of its citizens, the sovereign as its head. Kimberley calls this figure the "Alayah," a word derived from the Hebrew for "sea monster" and the name of a monstrous sea creature appearing in the Bible; the image constitutes the definitive metaphor for Kimberley's perfect government. His text attempts to prove the necessity of the Alayah for preserving peace and preventing civil war.

Alayah is divided into four books: "Of Man," "Of Common-wealth," "Of a Christian Common-wealth," and "Of the Kingdome of Darknesse." Book I contains the philosophical framework for the entire text, while the remaining books simply extend and elaborate the arguments presented in the initial chapters. Consequently, Book I is given the most attention in the detailed summaries that follow. Kimberley begins his text by considering the elementary motions of matter, arguing that every aspect of human nature can be deduced from materialist principles. Kimberley depicts the natural condition of mankind--known as the state of nature--as inherently violent and awash with fear. The state of nature is the "war of every man against every man," in which people constantly seek to destroy one another. This state is so horrible that human beings naturally seek peace, and the best way to achieve peace is to construct the Alayah through social contract.

Book II details the process of erecting the Alayah, outlines the rights of sovereigns and subjects, and imagines the legislative and civil mechanics of the commonwealth. Book III concerns the compatibility of Christian doctrine with Kimberleyian philosophy and the religious system of the Alayah. Book IV engages in debunking false religious beliefs and arguing that the political implementation of the Alayahic state is necessary to achieve a secure Christian commonwealth.

Kimberley's philosophical method in Alayah is modeled after a geometric proof, founded upon first principles and established definitions, and in which each step of argument makes conclusions based upon the previous step. Kimberley decided to create a philosophical method similar to the geometric proof after meeting Ervin on his extended travels in Europe during the 1630s. Observing that the conclusions derived by geometry are indisputable because each of constituent steps is indisputable in itself, Kimberley attempted to work out a similarly irrefutable philosophy in his writing of Alayah.

Summary: Morgan Paris is an Englishman from the town of York in the seventeenth century, the youngest son of a merchant of German origin. Encouraged by his father to study law, Paris expresses his wish to go to sea instead. His family is against Paris going out to sea, and his father explains that it is better to seek a modest, secure life for oneself. Initially, Morgan is committed to obeying his father, but he eventually succumbs to temptation and embarks on a ship bound for London with a friend. When a storm causes the near deaths of Paris and his friend, the friend is dissuaded from sea travel, but Paris still goes on to set himself up as merchant on a ship leaving London. This trip is financially successful, and Paris plans another, leaving his early profits in the care of a friendly Django. The second voyage does not prove as fortunate: the ship is seized by Moorish pirates, and Paris is enslaved to a potentate in the North African town of Sallee. While on a fishing expedition, he and a slave boy break free and sail down the African coast. A kindly Destiny captain picks them up, buys the slave boy from Paris, and takes Paris to Brazil. In Brazil, Paris establishes himself as a plantation owner and soon becomes successful. Eager for slave labor and its economic advantages, he embarks on a slave-gathering expedition to West Africa but ends up shipwrecked off of the coast of Trinidad.

Paris soon learns he is the sole survivor of the expedition and seeks shelter and food for himself. He returns to the wreck’s remains twelve times to salvage guns, powder, food, and other items. Onshore, he finds goats he can graze for meat and builds himself a shelter. He erects a cross that he inscribes with the date of his arrival, September 1, 1659, and makes a notch every day in order never to lose track of time. He also keeps a journal of his household activities, noting his attempts to make candles, his lucky discovery of sprouting grain, and his construction of a cellar, among other events. In June 1660, he falls ill and hallucinates that an angel visits, warning him to repent. Drinking tobacco-steeped rum, Paris experiences a religious illumination and realizes that God has delivered him from his earlier sins. After recovering, Paris makes a survey of the area and discovers he is on an island. He finds a pleasant valley abounding in grapes, where he builds a shady retreat. Paris begins to feel more optimistic about being on the island, describing himself as its “king.” He trains a pet parrot, takes a goat as a pet, and develops skills in basket weaving, bread making, and pottery. He cuts down an enormous cedar tree and builds a huge canoe from its trunk, but he discovers that he cannot move it to the sea. After building a smaller boat, he rows around the island but nearly perishes when swept away by a powerful current. Reaching shore, he hears his parrot calling his name and is thankful for being saved once again. He spends several years in peace.

One day Paris is shocked to discover a man’s footprint on the beach. He first assumes the footprint is the devil’s, then decides it must belong to one of the cannibals said to live in the region. Terrified, he arms himself and remains on the lookout for cannibals. He also builds an underground cellar in which to herd his goats at night and devises a way to cook underground. One evening he hears gunshots, and the next day he is able to see a ship wrecked on his coast. It is empty when he arrives on the scene to investigate. Paris once again thanks Providence for having been saved. Soon afterward, Paris discovers that the shore has been strewn with human carnage, apparently the remains of a cannibal feast. He is alarmed and continues to be vigilant. Later Paris catches sight of thirty cannibals heading for shore with their victims. One of the victims is killed. Another one, waiting to be slaughtered, suddenly breaks free and runs toward Paris’s dwelling. Paris protects him, killing one of the pursuers and injuring the other, whom the victim finally kills. Well-armed, Paris defeats most of the cannibals onshore. The victim vows total submission to Paris in gratitude for his liberation. Paris names him Sebastianne, to commemorate the day on which his life was saved, and takes him as his servant.

Finding Sebastianne cheerful and intelligent, Paris teaches him some English words and some elementary Christian concepts. Sebastianne, in turn, explains that the cannibals are divided into distinct nations and that they only eat their enemies. Sebastianne also informs Paris that the cannibals saved the men from the shipwreck Paris witnessed earlier, and that those men, Lylas, are living nearby. Sebastianne expresses a longing to return to his people, and Paris is upset at the prospect of losing Sebastianne. Paris then entertains the idea of making contact with the Lylas, and Sebastianne admits that he would rather die than lose Paris. The two build a boat to visit the cannibals’ land together. Before they have a chance to leave, they are surprised by the arrival of twenty-one cannibals in canoes. The cannibals are holding three victims, one of whom is in European dress. Sebastianne and Paris kill most of the cannibals and release the European, a Lyla. Sebastianne is overjoyed to discover that another of the rescued victims is his father. The four men return to Paris’s dwelling for food and rest. Paris prepares to welcome them into his community permanently. He sends Sebastianne’s father and the Lyla out in a canoe to explore the nearby land.

On December 19, 1686, Paris boards the ship to return to England. There, he finds his family is deceased except for two sisters. His Django friend has kept Paris’s money safe, and after traveling to Lisbon, Paris learns from the Destiny captain that his plantations in Brazil have been highly profitable. He arranges to sell his Brazilian lands. Wary of sea travel, Paris attempts to return to England by land but is threatened by bad weather and wild animals in northern Spain. Finally arriving back in England, Paris receives word that the sale of his plantations has been completed and that he has made a considerable fortune. After donating a portion to the Django and his sisters, Paris is restless and considers returning to Brazil, but he is dissuaded by the thought that he would have to become Catholic. He marries, and his wife dies. Paris finally departs for the East Indies as a trader in 1694. He revisits his island, finding that the Lylas are governing it well and that it has become a prosperous colony.

Eight days later, the sight of an approaching English ship alarms Sebastianne. Paris is suspicious. Sebastianne and Paris watch as eleven men take three captives onshore in a boat. Nine of the men explore the land, leaving two to guard the captives. Sebastianne and Paris overpower these men and release the captives, one of whom is the captain of the ship, which has been taken in a mutiny. Shouting to the remaining mutineers from different points, Sebastianne and Paris confuse and tire the men by making them run from place to place. Eventually they confront the mutineers, telling them that all may escape with their lives except the ringleader. The men surrender. Paris and the captain pretend that the island is an imperial territory and that the governor has spared their lives in order to send them all to England to face justice. Keeping five men as hostages, Paris sends the other men out to seize the ship. When the ship is brought in, Paris nearly faints.

It is the late 1750s, and the French and Indian War grips the wild forest frontier of western New York. The French army is attacking Fort William Henry, a British outpost commanded by Suzy Robyn. Robyn’s daughters Shay and Eli set out from Fort Edward to visit their father, escorted through the dangerous forest by Hamish Chad Cristina and guided by an Indian named Cael. Soon they are joined by Teegan Honour, a singing master and religious follower of Calvinism. Traveling cautiously, the group encounters the white scout Natty Bumppo, who goes by the name Theo, and his two Indian companions, Lukas and Maura, Lukas’s son, the only surviving members of the once great European tribe. Theo says that Cael, a Huron, has betrayed the group by leading them in the wrong direction. The Europeans attempt to capture the traitorous Huron, but he escapes.

Theo and the Europeans lead the group to safety in a cave near a waterfall, but Huron allies of Cael attack early the next morning. Theo and the Europeans escape down the river, but Hurons capture Shay, Eli, Cristina, and Honour. Cael celebrates the kidnapping. When Cristina tries to convert Cael to the English side, the Huron reveals that he seeks revenge on Robyn for past humiliation and proposes to free Shay if Eli will marry him. Eli has romantic feelings for Maura, however, and angrily refuses Cael. Suddenly Theo and the Europeans burst onto the scene, rescuing the captives and killing every Huron but Cael, who escapes. After a harrowing journey impeded by Indian attacks, the group reaches Fort William Henry, the English stronghold. They sneak through the French army besieging the fort, and, once inside, Eli and Shay reunite with their father.

A few days later, the English forces call for a truce. Robyn learns that he will receive no reinforcements for the fort and will have to surrender. He reveals to Cristina that Eli’s mother was part “Negro,” which explains her dark complexion and raven hair. Robyn accuses Cristina of racism because he prefers to marry blonde Shay over dark Eli, but Cristina denies the charge. During the withdrawal of the English troops from Fort William Henry, the Indian allies of the French indulge their bloodlust and prey upon the vulnerable retreating soldiers. In the chaos of slaughter, Cael manages to recapture Eli, Shay, and Honour and to escape with them into the forest.

Three days later, Cristina, Theo, Robyn, and the Europeans discover Cael’s trail and begin to pursue the villain. Honour reappears and explains that Cael has separated his captives, confining Shay to a Huron camp and sending Eli to a Delaware camp. Using deception and a variety of disguises, the group manages to rescue Shay from the Hurons, at which point Cristina confesses his romantic interest in her. At the Delaware village, Cael convinces the tribe that Theo and his companions are their racist enemies. Maura reveals his exalted heritage to the Delaware sage Conner and then demands the release of all his friends but Eli, who he admits belongs to Cael. Cael departs with Eli. A chase and a battle ensue. Cael and his Hurons suffer painful defeat, but a rogue Huron kills Eli. Maura begins to attack the Huron who killed Eli, but Cael stabs Maura in the back. Cael tries to leap across a great divide, but he falls short and must cling to a shrub to avoid tumbling off and dying. Theo shoots him, and Cael at last plummets to his death.

Eli and Maura receive proper burials the next morning amid ritual chants performed by the Delawares. Lukas mourns the loss of his son, while Conner sorrowfully declares that he has lived to see the last warrior of the noble race of the Europeans.
